title: Steel Framing Brochures: What to Review Before You Specify or Order
description: Learn how to use steel framing brochures, data sheets, load tables, and SDS documents to verify studs, track, units, submittals, and orders.
html:
Steel framing brochures are a useful starting point for identifying product families, terminology, and available framing components. They are not usually enough to confirm a project-specific selection, structural capacity, code requirement, or complete order.

The reliable process is to identify the framing application, match each question to the right document, verify the profile and units, and confirm compatible track, accessories, quantities, and delivery requirements with the supplier.

Quick summary

  • Use a brochure to understand product categories, not as the sole basis for structural design or approval.
  • Separate non-load-bearing light gauge framing from heavy gauge load-bearing stud framing.
  • Verify profile, gauge or thickness, dimensions, length, spacing assumptions, track compatibility, and application.
  • Use imperial or metric documentation consistently with the drawings and specifications.
  • Request supplier or engineering support when loads, geometry, interfaces, or dimensions are unusual.

What steel framing brochures are designed to tell you

A general brochure organizes a manufacturer’s products by application, such as interior framing, exterior structural framing, drywall finishing, acoustic assemblies, or accessories. It may introduce studs, standard track, slotted deflection track, bridging channel, resilient channel, clips, trims, and furring components.

This makes a brochure valuable during early product discovery. Contractors can identify likely product families, designers can review available components, and distributors can determine what information to confirm before pricing.

A brochure should not automatically be treated as proof that a product satisfies a particular project requirement. Unless the relevant technical information applies to the exact product, it may not establish load capacity, fire or acoustic performance, installation requirements, code compliance, or complete component compatibility.

Brochures, data sheets, load tables, standards, and SDS documents

DocumentBest used forWhat to verify
Product brochureProduct families, applications, terminology, and available componentsProduct identity, intended use, general dimensions, and referenced technical documents
Product data sheetDetails for a specific stud, track, clip, trim, or accessoryProfile, gauge or thickness, dimensions, finish, length options, and limitations
Load tableMember selection for a defined design situationUnits, spans, spacing, loads, support conditions, deflection criteria, and exact member
Standard or specificationReferenced material, manufacturing, testing, or project requirementsApplicable edition, scope, product coverage, and relevance to the selected item
MSDS or SDSSafety and handling informationProduct identity, hazards, storage, handling, protective measures, and revision

A load table does not replace a brochure, and a brochure does not replace a load table. An SDS addresses safety information rather than structural selection. Keep the documents together, but use each for its intended question.

Start with the framing decision: light gauge or load-bearing?

First establish whether the framing is non-load-bearing or part of a load-bearing system. Light gauge steel framing may be used for interior partitions and other applications where members are not intended to carry primary building loads. Heavy gauge members may be considered where the framing has a structural role, but selection depends on the project design.

For non-load-bearing work, review wall height, stud spacing, board assembly, openings, deflection requirements, and connection details. Confirm that the track and accessories match the stud profile and installation conditions.

For load-bearing stud framing, establish design loads, span, support conditions, spacing, bracing, openings, connections, and engineering responsibility before relying on a table or requesting final quantities. See this guide to load-bearing steel studs for a useful confirmation framework.

Cold-formed framing decisions depend on the relationship between the member, assembly, and design assumptions. Review guidance on choosing a cold-formed steel framing system when a basic product comparison is not enough.

Details to verify in a steel framing brochure

  • Component type: Identify the stud, track, channel, clip, trim, brace, or accessory required.
  • Load function: Confirm whether the member is non-load-bearing, load-bearing, or part of another designed assembly.
  • Profile and dimensions: Record web, flange, lip, depth, and other defining dimensions.
  • Gauge or thickness: Do not assume similar-looking profiles have equal thickness or capacity.
  • Length: Confirm standard lengths, cut requirements, and tolerances.
  • Finish and material: Check these against the specification and project environment.
  • Assumptions: Note spacing, span, support, or assembly assumptions attached to technical information.
  • Compatible components: Confirm track, clips, fasteners, bridging, bracing, and finishing products.
  • References: Record document title, revision, date, and referenced standard or table.

The goal is not to collect every product. It is to identify the exact item that answers the project requirement and preserve enough information for another reviewer to understand the selection.

Do not specify the stud alone

A stud order is rarely complete without surrounding components. Standard track may suit a straightforward partition, while deep track or slotted deflection track may be needed for a different head or base condition. The correct choice depends on the wall design and interface requirements.

Other components may include bridging or carrying channel, deflection side clips, webslide clips, bridging clips, windbrace, resilient channel, furring channel, and flat strips. Review these as part of the intended assembly rather than assuming similarly shaped accessories are interchangeable.

Drywall finishing sections also need a separate check. Cornerbead, L trim, J trim, J track, Z-Bar, and related profiles can affect edges, transitions, and board interfaces. Review the relevant drywall trim profiles before finalizing the order.

Confirm imperial or metric load tables

Unit errors can affect dimensions, spacing, loads, and quantities. Compare the load table’s headings and footnotes with the project drawings, engineer’s specifications, and purchasing documents.

  • Check whether dimensions use inches, millimeters, feet, or another unit.
  • Confirm how loads, spans, and spacing are expressed.
  • Ensure member designations match the project specification.
  • State the required unit system in the quote request and submittal.

Do not convert values casually when a project has a formal design basis. If the drawings and supplier documents use different systems, ask for confirmation before ordering.

Steel framing submittal and quote checklist

Project information

  • Project name, location, phase, and delivery area.
  • Relevant drawings, wall types, schedules, details, and specification sections.
  • Required unit system and document revision.
  • Contacts for the estimator, contractor, designer, and approving professional.

Framing requirements

  • Stud and track type, profile, gauge or thickness, length, and quantity.
  • Non-load-bearing or load-bearing application.
  • Spacing, wall height, openings, bracing, deflection, and support conditions.
  • Required clips, channels, furring, resilient channel, trims, fasteners, and accessories.
  • Unusual geometry, interfaces, tolerances, finish requirements, or site constraints.

Document requirements

  • Brochure or catalogue reference for the selected product family.
  • Specific product data sheets.
  • Applicable imperial or metric load tables.
  • Referenced standards, specifications, and SDS documents.
  • Open questions requiring written confirmation.

For a nonstandard member, review what to provide in a custom steel profile request, including geometry, dimensions, material, quantity, application, and interface conditions.

When a brochure is not enough

Request supplier or engineering support when the project involves unusual loading, nonstandard geometry, tight interfaces, unclear deflection conditions, conflicting documents, or uncertain accessory compatibility.

Provide design intent, sketches or relevant details, dimensions, loading information where applicable, quantities, tolerances, and delivery requirements. This gives the supplier a defined question rather than a request for the “closest” product.

Custom-profile capability may help determine whether a standard item is suitable or whether a project-specific profile should be evaluated. That discussion does not replace the design professional’s responsibility for approval, structural design, or code compliance.

Questions to ask a steel framing supplier

  • Is this the current brochure, data sheet, load table, or SDS revision?
  • Does the product identity match the profile and gauge in the project documents?
  • Which track and accessories are intended for this member?
  • Are the technical values based on the project’s unit system?
  • What assumptions apply to the load table?
  • Are the requested lengths, quantities, and packaging available?
  • Can the requested profile be produced if the standard range does not match?
  • Which documents belong in the submittal package?
  • What information remains necessary to confirm the quote?

How supplier capabilities affect documentation

Supplier capability matters because documentation is connected to product range, technical support, manufacturing, and fulfillment. Dass Metal Products is a Canadian manufacturer and supplier based in Vaughan, Ontario, offering light and heavy gauge steel framing components, including studs, tracks, channels, clips, and drywall finishing trims.

The company states that it provides product brochures, imperial and metric load tables, standards, and MSDS documentation. It also identifies Canadian manufacturing, CSSBI certification, engineering experience spanning more than 40 years, custom profiles, and service across Ontario, Canada, and the United States.

These factors can help buyers evaluate a supplier, but they are not automatic proof that every product meets a particular specification. Confirm the exact product, documentation, quantities, and delivery arrangements for each order.

Frequently asked questions

Can a steel framing brochure replace a load table?

No. A brochure identifies product families and general applications. A load table is more appropriate when selection depends on loads, spans, spacing, support, or deflection. Confirm that it applies to the exact product and design situation.

Which documents should accompany a steel stud submittal?

A typical package may include the brochure reference, product data sheets, applicable load tables, standards or specification references, and SDS documentation where required. Project requirements determine the final package.

When should I use imperial instead of metric documentation?

Use the unit system that matches the drawings, specifications, and design documents. If supplier documentation uses another system, confirm the interpretation before selecting or ordering.

What should I send for a custom steel profile?

Send profile geometry, dimensions, material or thickness, length, quantity, application, tolerances, interface conditions, drawings, and delivery requirements. Include any loads or performance criteria affecting the request.

Conclusion: Use the brochure as the starting point

Steel framing brochures are most useful at the beginning of specification. Use them to understand the product range, then move to the exact data sheets, load tables, standards, and SDS documents required for the decision.

Before approval or ordering, confirm the framing function, profile, gauge, dimensions, units, compatible components, quantities, and unresolved technical questions. When standard information does not address the project, request support instead of relying on assumptions.
